title: Art Tatum's pay and prejudice against disabled performers
summary: Tatum's top salary on 52nd Street, and how blindness hurt performers such as Roland Kirk.

story.theme_name: Race and segregation in the jazz life
story.community_name: Segregation on the road and the bandstand

blocks.x: It's too bad that someone like Grant didn't get Tatum earlier on. Maybe he would have been given the kind of, you know, presentation, you know, equal to his talent.
He never played -- you know, I mean --
Well, Tatum got the highest salary of any
jazz musician on the Street. He got $700.00 at the after Three Deuces and then sliding time. That was the first time that figure had been reached for a group, three guys.
But I just think about that Tatum should have been presented, you know, in concert, you know, like a concert artist.
Well, that's what he was, but at that period either with Alec Templeton, people were leary with performers with defects. If you were lame or blind or whatnot, they couldn't face you, Al Hibbler,
So now you got Ray Charles.

Right, but even in this era with Ray Charles, Roland Kirk had a lot of problems because he was blind, and, you know, he told stories about they hired him for a TV show, and they said they couldn't insure him because he might trip over something and whatever, and so he lost the job, you know, things like that.
Uh-huh, Well, these are some of the ingredients we're talking about as to how our jazz musician has to survive.
